_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: That is what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: [to the first tanna:] You say two generations below the guaranteed investment and no further, and I say that even until ten generations they are exempt. The same is true of more than ten, but he used this number, as is done in several places, and the verse also uses it, as it is written: “Even the tenth generation” (Deuteronomy 23:3), and they are forbidden forever. He needed to teach it this way, for had he taught, “Even the offspring of the offspring are exempt,” I would have said that it is only these that Rabban Gamliel [so Rashi’s text; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is meant] exempts, and no more: just as we heard that the first tanna exempts the offspring of the offspring, although they were not born from the gentile’s own animals, yet obligates the offspring of the offspring of the offspring to give their young to the priest, so too Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, though he exempts the offspring of the offspring, would obligate one generation further.
rashi:a1.2: But according to Rav Huna, who says the first tanna did not descend: to exempt later generations, for he exempts only the offspring of the guaranteed-investment animals, since they came out of the gentile’s own animals: why does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel need to say “until ten generations”? Let him say, “Even the offspring of the offspring are exempt,” and we would learn from it that just as he exempts the offspring of the offspring, although they did not come out of the gentile’s own animals, the same is true until ten generations.
rashi:a1.3: It refers to “he established”: to the case where he established the offspring in place of their mothers, where the first tanna does descend to exempt later generations.
gershom:a1.1: But according to Rav Huna, who says: the first tanna exempts only one generation, and the second is obligated at once, why does he [Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel] need to say “until ten”? Let him say, “The second is exempt too.”
gershom:a2.1: It refers to “he established offspring”: where the first tanna descends to later generations and exempts two generations; therefore he says that even until ten generations they are exempt.
rashi:a2.1: Say: “They and the offspring”: which implies two generations: they are offspring, and [there are] other offspring [born of them].
gershom:a3.1: A conclusive refutation of Rav Huna: for here [the mishna] implies as Rav Yehuda says.
rashi:a3.1: Say: “They and the offspring”: that is, they are the offspring themselves; do not read it as [a further generation of] offspring.
gershom:a4.1: Say: “They, the offspring, are exempt”: that is, they are the first offspring, and no more.
gershom:a5.1: A ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts is exempt, because it is a nidmeh [an animal that resembles another species].
gershom:a6.1: Until it is an ox and its firstborn is an ox: excluding a nidmeh.
rashi:a6.1: “Warmed with the fleece of my sheep”: so what is fit for warming is called “fleece [gez],” and what is not fit for warming is not called fleece. And this goat born of a ewe has tough wool, for goats’ wool is tough.
gershom:a7.1: Lambs whose wool is tough: for example, a ewe whose wool resembles goats’ wool, which is tough [the text has an unclear word here]; all the more so a goat born of a ewe is exempt, since it is not fit for warming.
tosafot:a6.1: But doesn’t he agree with what the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught, lambs whose wool is tough…: The Gemara could not have objected that a goat born of a ewe should be excluded by the verse from which goats’ hair is excluded (Ḥullin 137a), “to stand and to serve,” which requires something fit for [the priestly garments of] service and so excludes goats’ hair. For perhaps, since this animal is of a kind fit for that service, being the offspring of a ewe, that is enough.
gershom:a8.1: Let us see with regard to which halakha Rabbi Meir obligates.
tosafot:a7.1: With a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts and its father was a he-goat: It mentions “a goat of sorts” to teach a novelty: although the father’s seed was effective in changing the young into a goat like itself, even so the Rabbis are not concerned with the father’s seed. But when the Gemara objects, “Let them disagree about concern for the father’s seed in general,” it does not take this novelty into account.
gershom:a9.1: And its father was a he-goat: and one slaughtered it together with its father on one day.
rashi:a7.1: One is concerned for the father’s seed: if one slaughters the father and the young on one day. Therefore Rabbi Meir deems him liable: if he slaughtered it [the he-goat] and its daughter, he is liable, since this one resembles it.
rashi:a7.2: One is not concerned: [even] with a goat born of a goat, if he slaughtered it and its father on one day.
gershom:a10.1: Rabbi Meir obligates, for he is concerned for the father’s seed, and he counts it as “it and its young” even though the young does not trail after it, since it resembles its father.
gershom:a11.1: And the Rabbis exempt, for they assign it to its mother, and it does not resemble its mother.
rashi:a8.1: As Ḥananya and the Rabbis disagree: in Shechitat Ḥullin, in the chapter Oto VeEt Beno (Ḥullin 78b), where Ḥananya deems liable and the Sages exempt.
gershom:a12.1: If so: if they disagree about this, concern for the father’s seed, let them disagree about it in general, in the chapter Oto VeEt Beno, where Ḥananya and the Rabbis disagree about this very matter.
rashi:a9.1: With a ewe born of a ewe: and [in the parallel case] of a goat born of a ewe, it speaks of a goat born of a goat born of a ewe.
rashi:a11.1: And if you wish, say: with a ewe born of a goat born of a ewe: it teaches one case, a ewe born of a goat, and that goat was born of a ewe.
rashi:a11.2: Rabbi Meir obligates: to give it to the priest, for the ovine nature has returned to its place and it is not a nidmeh. And this “ewe born of a goat” is not literally a ewe [a female], for a female is not consecrated as a firstborn; rather it means one of the sheep kind.
gershom:a13.1: And if you wish, say: it is actually about the firstborn, with a ewe born of a goat, and that goat was born of a ewe. Rabbi Meir obligates: he holds that although a ewe born of a goat is a nidmeh, since its grandmother was a ewe, the ovine nature has returned to its place, the middle generation is set aside, and it counts as “it is a lamb and its firstborn is a lamb,” and it is obligated in the firstborn. And the Rabbis hold that since it is a nidmeh, we do not say that the ovine nature has returned to its place.
gershom:a14.1: For example, where it has some of the features: resembling its mother. Rabbi Meir, who obligates, is like the unattributed mishna, and the Sages who exempt are Rabbi Shimon, who requires its head and the majority of its body.
rashi:a13.1: Rabbi Meir concedes: although regarding the firstborn he holds that the ovine nature returns to its place, here we require that it be of the goat family since the six days of Creation.
tosafot:a13.1: With the goat of the New Moon: it mentions the first [of the goat offerings], and the same is true of the festival goats, for “one” is written of them too.
gershom:a15.1: A goat born of a female goat always [back through the generations], for it is written “one,” that is, the distinct one, coming from the six days of Creation, which never had a mother of another kind.
rashi:a15.1: That applies where it does not trace back through generations: that is, where it is a nidmeh not with respect to its mother’s mother but with respect to its mother herself, not resembling its mother. But where it traces back through generations, where with respect to its mother it is not a nidmeh, since it resembles its mother, but with respect to its mother’s mother it is a nidmeh, say no; this teaches us “one,” that we require the distinct one from the six days of Creation.
gershom:a16.1: Both are necessary: for had it been only from there, from “or a goat,” excluding a nidmeh, that would apply where it is disqualified because it does not trace back through generations to its family and its kind did not return to its place, such as a lamb born of a goat born of a goat always; for that reason it is a nidmeh.
gershom:a17.1: But where it traces back through generations: such as a lamb born of a goat born of a lamb, say it is not a nidmeh and is fit for the goat of the New Moon [so the text]. This teaches us “one,” the distinct one.
rashi:a15.2: And if from there [so Rashi’s heading; the note explains the case the Davidson English renders “had it been derived only from here”]: for had it written “one” and not written “goat,” I would have said that a nidmeh is disqualified only for an obligatory offering, such as the additional goat of the New Moon, which is obligatory, but for a gift offering it would be fit. As for its mentioning the goat of the New Moon, the same is true of the festival goats, of which “one” is written; it simply mentions the first of them all.
gershom:a18.1: And had it taught us only “one,” that would apply where a nidmeh is disqualified, as for an obligatory offering like the goat of the New Moon, which is obligatory; but for a vow or a gift offering, no. This teaches us “a bull or a sheep,” which speaks of a vow or a gift.
rashi:a16.1: For its wool: of a lamb that is not distinctly a lamb through its generations.
gershom:a19.1: Everyone concedes: even according to Rabbi Meir, who obligates, that one is not flogged for its wool on account of diverse kinds if he wore it together with linen.
rashi:a19.1: Just as an offering that has not changed: for a nidmeh is disqualified for an offering.
rashi:a20.1: But if so: since you count trellising over a fig tree as a change.
gershom:a20.1: So too libations that have not changed, and these have the scent of the fig. But if so: if you count trellising as a change, flax too can be changed by trellising, and all these teachings of Rav Aḥa [so Gershom; the daf reads Rabbi Aḥa bar Yaakov], Rav Pappa and Rav [Naḥman bar Yitzḥak] are undone, since we find that flax too changes. Rather, conclude from this that trellising is not a change.
rashi:a20.2: This one, its scent has changed: the wine of that vine.
gershom:a21.1: Actually, trellising is a change; but with wine it counts as a change because its scent has changed, and a change of scent disqualifies it for libations. Trellising flax, however, is not a change, since a change in its scent does not matter for it.
gershom:a22.1: Both go to the priest: for it is possible to coincide precisely, so that both came out as one.
rashi:a21.2: It is impossible to coincide precisely: that both heads came out as one; rather, one came out first, and we do not know which one it is.
rashi:a22.1: And Rabbi Tarfon: explains and says: [the priest] chooses the better one. The Gemara explains the reason.
gershom:a23.1: Rabbi Tarfon says: the priest chooses the better one for himself, as the Gemara explains, that the healthy one comes out first.
gershom:a26.1: He chooses the better one for himself: as stated in the Gemara, that the one [born first] is the better.
rashi:a22.2: They assess between them: the Gemara explains that the priest takes the lean one.
gershom:a24.1: Rabbi Akiva says: they assess between them. Meaning: whichever of them takes the better one pays the other half of what it is worth more than the other.
gershom:a27.1: Rabbi Akiva says: they assess between them: as the Gemara explains, the “fat” [the extra value] is to be between them, and the Israelite takes the better one.
rashi:a22.3: And the second: which remains with the Israelite, grazes until it becomes blemished, and afterward it is eaten, since it is a possible firstborn; therefore it is not slaughtered unblemished. Of the priest’s lamb he did not need to say this, since it is certainly not slaughtered until it has a blemish, for the mishna speaks of the present time. Alternatively, it speaks of the time of the Temple, and the priest’s lamb is not fit to be sacrificed, since it is only a possible firstborn and there is a concern of [bringing] non-sacred animals into the Temple courtyard; therefore it too is eaten with its blemish. The reason it says that the Israelite’s lamb grazes until it becomes blemished is that it wants to say “and it is obligated in the gifts,” which applies to the Israelite, whereas a priest is entirely exempt from the gifts, as explained in Shechitat Ḥullin, in the chapter HaZero’a VeHaLeḥayayim (Ḥullin 132a). Therefore the whole mishna is taught about the Israelite. But the priest’s lamb too grazes until it becomes blemished, and he eats it with its blemish.
gershom:a25.1: And the second: the one in the Israelite’s hand is a possible firstborn; it grazes until it becomes blemished, that is, the Israelite may not eat it unblemished but only with its blemish. And it is obligated in the gifts, as the Gemara explains, because the priest comes at him from two sides.
rashi:b1.1: And obligated in the gifts: when he slaughters it he gives the priest the foreleg and the jaw [and the maw]. And this is an unattributed mishna.
rashi:b1.2: And Rabbi Yosei exempts: the Gemara explains [why].
gershom:b1.1: Rabbi Yosei exempts: from the gifts, as the Gemara explains, since its exchange is in the priest’s hand, and the Rabbis treated it as though the priest had sold it to him with its blemish.
rashi:b1.3: They divide: Rabbi Tarfon retracted what he said above, as the Gemara explains, for he holds that even while they are alive they raise the better one in value for both of them, so that they divide both; therefore, if one of them died, they divide the living one.
gershom:b2.1: One of them died: that is, he had not managed to give [one] to the priest before one died; they divide the living one.
gershom:b3.1: Rabbi Akiva says: they do not divide; rather it belongs to the Israelite, unless the priest brings proof that it was the firstborn.
rashi:b1.4: A male and a female, the priest has nothing here: for perhaps the female came out first, and the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. Here even Rabbi Tarfon agrees: there he disagrees because one of them certainly belongs to the priest, so the priest’s position is strong enough to divide equally; but here his position is weaker, since perhaps firstborn status does not apply at all. It must, however, graze until it becomes blemished, and afterward he eats it, since it is a case of uncertainty.
tosafot:b1.1: A male and a female, the priest has nothing: this applies even where the two heads came out as one, and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili concedes here. For even if both are consecrated when they open the whole womb [together], nevertheless one kind does not interpose before its own kind, as said in the first chapter (above, 9b); here, since the female also opens the womb as it does, its firstborn status is entirely void. This is unlike the case in the chapter Behema HaMaksha (Ḥullin 70a), where its sister wrapped around it and brought it out, for there it speaks of where he came out head first and she came out feet first, so that she did not open the womb.
gershom:b4.1: A male and a female, the priest has nothing here: for it is not known which came out first; it grazes until it becomes blemished and is eaten by its owners with its blemish.
gershom:b5.1: Two males and a female, where one [ewe] bore a male and the other bore a male and a female: one goes to the priest either way, and one is his [the owner’s], since it is not known whether the male came out first or the female.
gershom:b6.1: Rabbi Yosei says: whatever its exchange is in the priest’s hand [is exempt from the gifts]. And this too counts as an exchange in the priest’s hand: if they became intermingled, both are possible firstborns, since of each one may say, perhaps this one was born after the female. Therefore, when the priest takes one, the other is its exchange, and it is exempt from the gifts. And Rabbi Meir obligates, since [the priest] comes at him from two sides. Two females and a male, where one bore a female and the second a male and a female, or each bore a male and a female: the priest has nothing here.
rashi:b2.1: Gemara. It is possible to coincide precisely in the hands of Heaven: such as this birth, even though no one is particular about it.
rashi:b2.2: And all the more so in human hands: where people intend to make some measure or some thing precise, it is certainly possible to be precise.
gershom:b7.1: And all the more so in human hands: when a person intends to be precise, dividing something equally, he can be precise.
rashi:b2.3: In human hands: where people intend and measure in order to be precise, what? Is it possible to be precise or not?
tosafot:b2.1: In brief: Rashi explained “in the hands of Heaven” as a birth like this one, where no one is particular, and “in human hands” as where people intend to measure precisely. The Ri asks: how can the Gemara resolve the Rabbis’ view of human hands from a corpse found precisely between two towns? Even if people can measure precisely, the corpse’s position is itself in the hands of Heaven, since it fell there by itself. The Ri answers that even those who say precision in the hands of Heaven is impossible agree it sometimes happens; they mean only that it cannot be verified, as with a birth, where there is no time to check which came first. In human hands there is time to check, and the proof is: if verification were impossible, two heifers would not be brought out of doubt for so rare an event. At the end the Gemara concludes that for the Rabbis precision is impossible even in human hands. Tosafot then weigh the halakha. The Amoraic disputes about a breach equal to the standing wall (Eruvin 16b) and a half-and-half cut in slaughter (Ḥullin 28b) suggest the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei HaGelili at least in human hands; Gittin 78a does not contradict this. Shevuot 32a and Yevamot 28a, according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, suggest it does not follow him; so the Ri concludes: not in the hands of Heaven, yes in human hands. They raise Eruvin 5b (Rav Ashi on an alley of eight cubits, where equality is treated as a rabbinic doubt), and answer that one could measure, but the Sages did not trouble to for a rare case that is only rabbinic. They cite and dispute the reading of Rabbi Shimon of Joinville, that those Amoraic rulings follow the Rabbis. They set aside Sukka 15b on the readings of Rabbeinu Ḥananel, Rabbeinu Shimon and Rabbeinu Tam. Finally they discuss sources that seem to follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili even in the hands of Heaven: two animals that came out as the tenth (below, 60b; questioned in Eruvin 50a and Kiddushin 51a), “under its mother” (Ḥullin 38b), and Rava’s dilemma on going by the majority of limbs (Ḥullin 70a), and suggest how the first may be deflected. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b3.1: Encircles it: [the red line girds] the altar at the middle of its height.
rashi:b3.2: He puts: upper blood, which is to be put above the midpoint, he puts below; for perhaps they did not measure precisely and made the line well below the midpoint, and when they put upper blood a little above the line, one can say it is below the midpoint.
rashi:b3.3: And lower blood above: for perhaps they placed the line above the midpoint.
gershom:b8.1: Sometimes he puts: upper blood below and lower blood above, because that line was thin and it is impossible to be precise, so that it does not reach into either the upper five cubits or the lower five cubits, since it is impossible to be precise.
rashi:b3.4: One widens it a little: it is indeed impossible to be precise, but here they made the line wide: after measuring and beginning it at the middle, they widened it downward and upward, so that either way, what is below it is the lower part of the altar and what is above it is the upper part, with no doubt at all.
gershom:b9.1: No: indeed it is impossible to be precise. Do you think the line was thin? It was wide, and it extended somewhat into the upper five cubits and somewhat into the lower. Therefore there is no difficulty at all.
rashi:b4.1: Come and hear from the measurements of vessels: for the Merciful One says, “And you shall make a table” (Exodus 25:23); evidently they measured precisely and made it with its exact cubits.
gershom:b10.1: From the measurements of vessels, from the measurements of the altar, etc.: which have two and a half cubits; evidently one must be precise to that measure; conclude from this that it is possible to be precise in human hands.
rashi:b4.2: It is different there, as the Merciful One says, do it, and wherever you can do it, it pleases Him: and actually they did not measure precisely.
rashi:b4.3: “All this in writing, as the Lord has made me wise by His hand upon me”: David said this verse of all the work of the pattern. We do not read it here [in the Gemara].
gershom:b11.1: Nothing can be learned from here, for the Merciful One said: do as you are able, as precisely as you can aim, even though it is not complete precision, for He gave a measure only as a general instruction, as it is written: “All this in writing…”
rashi:b5.1: He divided it in two: an oven that became impure, and he divided it in two, and they are equal: they are impure, since it is impossible to be precise, and of each one may say that here is the majority; and we hold that the remnants of an oven [are impure] with its majority, in [the chapter] HaOr VeHaRotev (Ḥullin 124a).
gershom:b12.1: He divided it in two: the earthenware oven, and they are equal.
gershom:b13.1: Both are impure: the pieces, for of each one we say that it is more than the other half, since it is impossible for people to be precise in dividing with complete precision.
rashi:b5.2: And it has indentations: it does not divide evenly; when it is broken, pieces protrude from it and make a hollow here, and so in many places; therefore those protrusions cannot be measured.
gershom:b14.1: No, an oven is different, being an earthenware vessel: since it has indentations at the place of the break, which take from this part to that and from that to this, it is impossible to be precise with it, and both are impure.
rashi:b6.1: Found: a slain person precisely between two towns, so that neither is any closer to it than the other.
rashi:b7.1: It is possible to be precise: and to measure well; they determined that both are equally close. And he holds that “the nearest” written in the verse (Deuteronomy 21:3), “nearest to the slain,” implies even [two] nearest, so that if two are equally near to it, both break a heifer’s neck. For if it were impossible to be precise, then certainly one is nearer than the other; why would they bring two heifers? Let them bring one in partnership, as we say below: they give it, and the people of one town say, “If you are nearer to it than we are, let our share be given over to you and let it atone for you; and if we are nearer than you, let your share be ours and let it atone for us.”
gershom:b15.1: Because he holds that it is possible to be precise in human hands: for measuring is in human hands, [so it can be found] equally close to both. And where it is written “the nearest,” say even “the nearest ones,” so that both bring.
